titleStmt.title: Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the Mission in Geneva

div.head: 449. Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the Mission in Geneva
div.p: Secto 4020. Subject: Secretary’s meeting with Uruguayan President-elect Sanguinetti.

2. Summary: During one-hour meeting with President Sanguinetti Secretary congratulated Sanguinetti on the return to democracy in Uruguay, and promised our support. Sanguinetti made special plea for support in economic area and for help in closing UNHCR books on Uruguay. He said Central America was special problem, and GOU policy would be based on quest for peace and justice. He expressed concern that Central America, and especially Ortega’s request to meet with Secretary in Uruguay, not become an issue in our relations.

3. Sanguinetti opened the meeting by explaining the importance of this day to Uruguay. Uruguay has the oldest democratic tradition in Latin America, and the re-establishment of democratic institutions is important not only here but throughout the region. But democracy would not solve all problems, especially the economic ones. The policies of the new government would be moderate. He anticipated good relations with the U.S. and asked for support and understanding, especially in the economic area. He emphasized the need for investment and market access, but acknowledged the legal constraints on our policies. He noted that Uruguay’s economy had declined dramatically in the past three years, and it would be difficult for the people to accept new austerity programs. He made a commitment to seek agreement with the IMF, World Bank and commercial banks. He emphasized that to pay debt Uruguay must export, to export, Uruguay must have investment.

4. In foreign policy, Uruguay would not depart from traditional lines. The GOU would join no bloc, support peace and maintain relations with other nations on a non-ideological basis. Agreement had been reached to re-established relations with Venezuela, and discussions have started with Cuba. He recognized the risks of relations with Cuba, and would establish clear limits on their presence and activities in Uruguay.

5. On Central America, the GOU would support international law and peace. Ortega of Nicaragua seeks relations with GOU,
seeks a meeting with U.S. in Montevideo. The GOU does not want to mediate between the Nicaraguans and U.S. in any meeting in Montevideo.

6. In his response, the Secretary noted the importance of March first as the day democracy returned to Uruguay. He promised U.S. support and understanding because of the special importance of the return to democracy in Latin America for President Reagan and the USG. The Secretary recognized the special importance of economic recovery to the preservation of democracy, agreed growth was the answer to the debt and recession problems, and reiterated our promise of support. He said there were limits on what we can do, but offered to cooperate in any possible way. Most important to recovery, however, were GOU policies.

7. The U.S. is the most open market in the world, continued the Secretary. Citing figures on the increase of Uruguayan exports to the U.S., he said we are already doing a lot. We are not protectionist, but have some problems in special areas, such as textiles.

8. The Secretary delivered a letter from President Reagan inviting President Sanguinetti to make a state visit to the U.S. later this year. He explained that the invitation was not only important as a symbol of our support for Uruguay, but also would enable Sanguinetti to convey a message to U.S. businessmen and investors. He promised to do everything we can to make the trip a success.
9. Sanguinetti expressed appreciation for the invitation and reiterated his interest in good relations with the U.S.

10. In the area of human rights, Sanguinetti said the problem was solved for Uruguay. He said the issue of human rights in Uruguay was being considered this week in Geneva by the UNHCR and asked for our support in closing the books on Uruguay. He said the matter was urgent because if no decisions were reached this week, Uruguay would be maintained on the UN’s problem list for some time to come. He asked for our support.

11. Returning to the problem of Nicaragua, the Secretary said we had received no request for a meeting in Montevideo. He said we would meet if requested, but emphasized he was here in Montevideo to celebrate the return of democracy, not to meet with Ortega. The presence of Ortega in Montevideo on this occasion was ironic because Nicaragua was one of the few exceptions to the return of democracy in Latin America. With respect to relations with Cuba, the Secretary said this was a Uruguayan decision. He warned of the risks, however, and noted that Cuba uses embassies as a base for interfering in the internal affairs of the host country. He offered to provide information on this if requested.

12. In closing, the Secretary reiterated our support for democracy in Uruguay. We want to find ways to help the new GOU within our limitations. He said the U.S. wanted to work with the GOU on specific ideas for cooperation in the economic area, and said consultations could begin soon. Sanguinetti responded the GOU was working on specific ideas
as well and looked forward to discussions.

13. As the meeting broke up, Assistant Secretary Motley returned to the problem of Nicaragua. He said we had received no request for a meeting, the U.S. delegation and the Nicaraguan delegation were in the same hotel, and we would be ready to meet provided the request didn’t come too late. Foreign Minister Iglesias said he would convey this message to the Nicaraguans.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850142–0520. Secret; Immediate; Exdis. Shultz was in Montevideo March 1–2 to attend Sanguinetti’s inauguration.

In telegram 7339 from Montevideo, November 30, 1984, Aranda reported that he had called Sanguinetti to congratulate him on his election and “alert him to the coming call for consultations on another wool textile category,” to which Sanguinetti reacted “sullenly.” Aranda commented: “I can fully understand Sanguinetti’s deep disappointment that our first major action in the economic field following his victory should be another call for textile consultations, especially in light of his election-eve plea to Uruguay’s democratic friends abroad to keep their markets open to Uruguay’s products.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840767–0497) In a February 8 memorandum to McFarlane, Tillman wrote: “You should be aware that we have gotten off to a rather shaky start with the new civilian government in Uruguay…over trade consultations about textiles.” (Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Subject File, Uruguay)

In telegram Secto 4021 from Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation, March 2, Shultz wrote to Reagan that during his meeting that morning, Sanguinetti accepted Reagan’s invitation for a State visit. Shultz noted: “I conveyed our policy of support for democracy in Uruguay and throughout the hemisphere. Sanguinetti seems genuinely committed to democracy, to rational economic policies and to good relations with us. He intends however to have normal diplomatic relations with both Cuba and Nicaragua. I warned him that we considered both to be enemies of democracy and that there internal risks associated with this policy.” (Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 51G, Uruguay) Reagan’s February 27 letter to Sanguinetti is in the Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Subject File, Uruguay.
